name: Satawalese
confidence_why: The only explicit statement is one hedged sentence in Kikusawa 2018's orthography note (heaviest stress on the last syllable, highest pitch on the penult, no contrastive accent); Roddy 2007's sketch grammar says nothing about stress and Jackson 1983 reconstructs penultimate-mora stress for Proto-Trukic, so final placement is the best reading but rests on thin evidence.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not contrastive. In citation forms (word in isolation, normal tempo) the strongest stress is on the final syllable, while the pitch peak sits on the penultimate syllable; the source hedges with 'usually'.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated beyond the hedge 'usually'; no interaction with vowel length or geminates is described, although the same section notes that all vowels contrast length and all consonants except y and w occur as geminates.
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly the word uttered in isolation (citation form); nothing on phrase-level stress or connected speech. The statement is a two-sentence note in the orthography front matter of a cultural dictionary, resting on Sugita Hiroshi's 1980s phonological analysis and Kikusawa's own work with speakers (2005-2018); no instrumental study. Roddy's 2007 sketch grammar, the only Glottolog-listed description, is silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The 2018 Satawalese Cultural Dictionary describes the Satawalese of Satawal Island proper (sata1237), from 1978-82 fieldwork with senior speakers (informants incl. Isidore Namonur) and compiler Sabino Sauchomal; the Introduction notes some East/West lexical variants on the island but no dialect split. Satawalese is also a source variety of southern Saipan Carolinian (caro1242), which is a different language.

One tension worth recording: Jackson 1983 (p. 223) reconstructs Proto-Trukic with alternating stress anchored on the penultimate mora, whereas Kikusawa 2018 reports for modern Satawalese words in isolation the heaviest stress on the last syllable with the highest pitch on the penult, after stating that meaning-distinguishing stress or pitch accent is not observed. sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in
sources.note: Chapter 2 'Sounds of the language' (pp. 17-34) covers consonants, vowels, contrastive vowel length (2.3.2), low vowel dissimilation, syllable structure (C)(C)V(V)(C) and phonotactics; the text has no occurrence of 'stress', 'accent' or 'prosod' anywhere in 212 pp. Silent on stress. Its bibliography (pp. 191-199) lists Jackson 1983, E. Quackenbush 1968, H. Quackenbush 1970, Sudo & Sauchomal 1982, Tiucheimal 1980, McCoy & McCoy 1990.

sources.citation: Kikusawa, Ritsuko. 2018. Introduction. In Satawalese Cultural Dictionary, pp. xiii-xvii. Osaka: National Museum of Ethnology.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Provenance: data from Satawal fieldwork 1978-80 by Akimichi, Ishimori, Sudo; Sugita Hiroshi did the 'preliminary grammatical and phonological analysis' (reported in Sudo & Sauchomal 1981); native compiler Sabino Sauchomal 1981-82; 'accented vowels' (á é í ó ú) in the earlier orthography are vowel-quality marks, not stress marks; some East/West regional variants noted.
